title: Chidi and the Thirteenth Hour
blurb: A brass clock with thirteen numbers gives Chidi an extra hour every day. But every hour has an owner.

chapters.title: The Clock with Thirteen Numbers
chapters.text:
Chidi never had enough time. His school day in Lagos began at seven, football practice ended at five, and then came homework, chores and his little sister Ngozi, who needed help with her violin. By bedtime, Chidi was always behind.

One Saturday, he wandered into the repair shop at the end of his street. Mr Okonkwo, a thin man with silver glasses, was sitting among hundreds of ticking clocks. "Looking for something?" he asked.

"A way to get more time," joked Chidi.

Mr Okonkwo smiled strangely. From a dusty shelf, he took down a small brass clock. Chidi looked closer and blinked. The face had thirteen numbers instead of twelve.

"It is broken," Chidi said.

"Very likely," said Mr Okonkwo. "Take it. It is free. But be careful. Time is not as simple as it looks."

chapters.title: The Extra Hour
chapters.text:
That night, Chidi put the clock on his shelf and tried to sleep. At exactly midnight, the clock began to chime: one, two, three... all the way to thirteen.

At the thirteenth chime, the whole world stopped. The ceiling fan hung still in mid-spin. A moth froze in the air near the window. Outside, a car stood silent on the road with its headlights shining.

Chidi crept to the window. Nothing moved. He was the only one awake in a world of statues.

"Whoa," he whispered. "An extra hour!"

He used it well. He finished his maths homework, practised passing the football against the wall, and even read half a book. When the hour was over, the clock ticked once, and the world started again. The moth flew on. Chidi fell asleep smiling.

chapters.title: Too Good to Stop
chapters.text:
For a week, the clock chimed thirteen every midnight. Chidi's life changed. He finished his homework early, his football improved, and his teacher praised his neat work. He even had time to play cards with his friends in the evening.

"How do you do it?" asked his best friend, Emeka.

"Just good planning," Chidi lied.

But he began to notice something odd. Ngozi was always tired now. At breakfast she yawned over her porridge, and during violin practice her bow slid off the strings. "I do not know what is wrong," she said sadly. "I sleep all night, but I wake up exhausted."

Chidi felt a tiny cold feeling in his stomach. He thought about the clock. Then he pushed the thought away. After all, it could not possibly be connected.

chapters.title: The Clockmaker's Warning
chapters.text:
The next evening, Ngozi fell asleep in the middle of her violin practice. Chidi carried her to bed. Then he took the brass clock in his bag and ran down the street to the repair shop.

Mr Okonkwo was waiting at the door, as if he had expected him. "I wondered when you would come," he said. "You have noticed, then."

"Noticed what?" Chidi's voice shook.

"The clock does not make time," said the old man. "It only moves it. Every extra hour you use is taken from somebody close to you. Somebody who loves you, and whom you love. They lose an hour of rest and do not know why."

Chidi felt his legs go weak. "Ngozi," he whispered. "I have been taking her hours."

"Yes. And there is only one way to stop it," said Mr Okonkwo. "You must give back all the hours you have taken."

chapters.title: Giving It Back
chapters.text:
"But how?" asked Chidi. "I cannot just hand her seven hours."

"You can spend your hours on her," said Mr Okonkwo. "Time is not given back by a magic trick. It is given back by care. For every hour you borrowed, give an hour of your own time to Ngozi, and do it gladly. When you have repaid them all, the clock will stop."

Chidi took a deep breath and ran home. That night, he put the clock aside, and for the next week he got up early. He helped Ngozi with her scales. He carried her violin to school. He sat in the front row at her lessons and clapped louder than anyone.

Some days, his homework was late and football practice was missed. It was not easy. But when Ngozi laughed again, Chidi found that he did not mind.

chapters.title: Twelve Is Enough
chapters.text:
On Saturday evening, Ngozi played at the school concert. Her bow danced over the strings, and the hall was silent until the last note. When she finished, the audience stood up and cheered. In the front row, Chidi clapped until his hands hurt.

That night at midnight, the clock chimed twelve times. Only twelve. Nothing stopped, and the moth outside kept on flying. Chidi smiled in the dark.

The next morning, he took the clock back to Mr Okonkwo. "Keep it," said the old man. "Or use it as a lesson. Time is the only thing that we all have in equal amounts."

"I think I understand," said Chidi. "I never needed more hours. I needed to use the ones I had."

On the way home, he wrote a timetable on the back of his hand: homework, football, Ngozi. Then he looked at the sky and noticed that twelve hours were plenty.
